articles.text:
Volume 2, Number 11.

Bad Lands Cow Boy, By A. T. Packard.

The Cow Boy is not published for fun, but for $2 per year.

Advertising Rates made known on application. Standing Advertisements payable quarterly. Transient Advertisements and all Job work, money in sight.

Address all communications to The Bad Lands Cow Boy, Medora, Dakota.

Entered at the post-office at Medora, Dak., as second class mail matter.
articles.summary: Masthead, volume number and publication terms; front-page dateline reads Medora, Dakota, April 16, 1885.

articles.summary: Directory of display advertisements filling columns 1–4 of the front page.

articles.text: Bismarck's recent election was, on the whole, a Democratic victory. John A. Carland was elected mayor and the majority of the city council is also Democratic.
articles.summary: Bismarck's city election went Democratic, with John A. Carland elected mayor.

articles.text: General Grant still hangs on to life, although death cannot be very far away. It is now hoped by the physicians that they can keep him alive until death comes from the cancer, which may be a month yet.
articles.summary: Note on General Grant's illness.

articles.text: That bulls are scarce in the round-up is simply because they are scarce on the range. We doubt if to-day there is an average on the river of four bulls to the hundred cows. Our cowmen will remedy this difficulty soon by the addition of three or four more to the hundred.
articles.summary: The paper says bulls are scarce on the Little Missouri, about four to the hundred cows.

articles.text: The farce of trying to elect a U. S. senator for Illinois is still going on in the legislature of that state. In the whole history of our government we do not know of a more useless session of the legislature or more uncalled-for waste of the peoples' money.
articles.summary: Editorial on the deadlocked Illinois senatorial election.

articles.text: There remains scarcely any doubt that England and Russia will soon have a war. Taking into consideration the many advantages such a war will confer on the United States, we can scarcely say we are sorry at the prospect. Already is the effect manifest both in the beef and shipping trades.
articles.summary: Editorial on a likely Anglo-Russian war and its effect on the beef trade.

articles.text: Some of the large factories in the east are having serious times with their employes. The workmen in the McCormick reaper works in Chicago are on a strike. There has been considerable shooting but only one man was killed. Much enmity has been aroused toward Pinkerton's police and serious trouble is feared.
articles.summary: Note on the McCormick reaper works strike in Chicago.

articles.text: The Riel rebellion has now become a serious matter. Strong efforts are being made to induce the Dominion government to accede to the perfectly just and reasonable demands of the rebels, but with the bull-headed obstinacy characteristic of the English, they seem to prefer force to justice. The cause of the rebels is almost hopeless but they can be assured of the hearty good wishes of all on this side of the line.
articles.summary: Editorial sympathizing with the Riel rebellion in Canada.

articles.text: Spread-eagle Harrison has about reached the end of his rope in Chicago politics. He was recently supposed to be elected mayor by a very small majority. It has turned out that there were numerous frauds committed and the result is liable to be reversed. At any event, it has been made plainly manifest that all kinds of frauds have been practiced by the Harrison-McDonald gang, even to the stealing of the ballot-boxes and a committee of public safety has been organized, consisting of Republicans and Democrats, with the avowed purpose of sifting the matter to the bottom. For the good of Chicago it is to be hoped that Harrison will be ousted.
articles.summary: Editorial on alleged frauds in Carter Harrison's Chicago mayoral election.

articles.headline: Additional Local.
articles.text: Wm. VanDriesche returned Monday evening.
articles.summary: Wm. VanDriesche returned to Medora Monday evening.

articles.text: Doc. Pennell loaded and pulled for the Hills last Saturday with a lot of tree sprouts and shrubs.
articles.summary: Doc. Pennell left for the Black Hills with tree sprouts and shrubs.

articles.text: It is perfectly impossible to even imagine more perfect weather than that with which we have been blessed lately. We would be willing to exchange some of it, though, for rain.
articles.summary: Fine dry weather; rain wanted.

articles.text: The Willard Bros. will probably be here to-morrow with eighty head of cow-horses, which they hope to sell on the river. They will then get another bunch for the Hills.
articles.summary: The Willard Bros. expected with eighty cow-horses for sale.

articles.text: Dr. Jorgens will move into his new building the first of next week. He will soon open up a full line of crockery in addition to his drug stock. The building is 24x32 and is to have a full glass front.
articles.summary: Dr. Jorgens to move his drug store into a new 24x32 building.

articles.text: The slaughter house is nearly ready for business and it is hoped that fat cattle enough can be found to start up by May 1. We scarcely see where they are coming from however, until June 1, at the earliest.
articles.summary: Medora slaughter house nearly ready; hopes to start by May 1.

articles.text: The bull round-up south of the track began Tuesday. Davis, Sully, Andrews and Garner creeks have been worked and to-day the country around D. K. Wade's will be rounded-up. Not a half a dozen dead animals have been found and bulls also are scarce.
articles.summary: Bull round-up south of the railroad began Tuesday; few dead animals found.

articles.text: Some one is missing the opportunity of a life-time by not starting a butter and cheese factory here. All the fresh cows wanted could be had for the keeping and ready sale could be found here and on the road for all the product. Who possesses the capital and experience to start in?
articles.summary: The paper urges someone to start a butter and cheese factory at Medora.

articles.text: Some tenderfoot has sent us an article on roller skating, copied almost entire from an article which has been floating around the newspaper world until it has become stale, and signed it "Cow-puncher." We don't really think the writer knows the difference between a hackamore and a round-up and that he does know a great deal more about rubbing stage stock. We like to hear from you, boys, but write original articles and send your names so that the editor may know whom to get action on, provided he happens to get stepped on for publishing some other man's ideas.
articles.summary: Packard rebukes a contributor who sent in a plagiarized roller-skating article signed "Cow-puncher."

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES. Strayed or Stolen.
articles.text: From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: Notice of a bay horse belonging to John Pohl strayed or stolen from Little Missouri in July 1884; $25 reward.

articles.text: The Little Missouri round-up begins May 25.
articles.summary: The Little Missouri round-up will begin May 25.

articles.text: Six weeks from to-day the ranges will be covered with cattle, rolling in fat from this year's grass.
articles.summary: Prediction of fat cattle on the range in six weeks.

articles.text: By a resolution proposed by Mr. Towers, horseracing or anything else detrimental to the morals of cow camps are prohibited on the ranches of members of the Wyoming association.
articles.summary: Wyoming association bans horseracing at members' cow camps on Mr. Towers' resolution.

articles.text: Even though we have not had much rain, the grass is coming up finely, much of it being already three inches long. For about a month the cattle will run down on it but will then pick up rapidly.
articles.summary: Grass already three inches long around Medora.

articles.text: The meeting of the Wyoming Stock-growers' association, at Cheyenne brought out many interesting points. The secretary's report on contagious diseases had to handle the subject with gloved hands as many of the principal members of the Wyoming association are prominent cowmen of Texas. Nevertheless it put forth many facts that conclusively proved the great danger of driving cattle from Texas into the north, without a quarantine of at least sixty days. The Territorial veterinarian, Dr. Hopkins, has made thorough examination and it was conclusively proved that every herd that crossed the trail made by Texas cattle lost from three to one hundred per cent., the latter loss being an entire herd of valuable bulls. There was no herd that crossed the trail, which did not lose some of its members, even after cold weather set in. In every case the fatal disease was unquestionably Splenic, commonly called Texas fever, and it was equally as certain that the losses all came from crossing the trail made by Texas cattle. The secretary's report recommended that Texas cattle be allowed to come north after a quarantine of sixty days, as at the end of that time all danger was over. In reference to contagious pleuro-pneumonia, the report stated that the disease had appeared in four states further west than ever before, viz: Ohio, Illinois, Kentucky and Missouri. One infected herd had also been taken to Tennessee and one to Texas, but there are as yet no outside cases in either of these states. It was strongly recommended that all eastern cattle be quarantined until it is certain they are free from disease. "Speaking without heat or prejudice" the secretary then showed the difference between the two national meetings held at Chicago and St. Louis. He stated that the Chicago meeting held in April was of perfect fairness, that it desired above all things to harmonize all conflicting interests and enroll all cattlemen in one grand national association. To this end only a partial list of officers was elected the remaining to be elected by the St. Louis meeting. A committee on consolidation then went to the St. Louis meeting but the idea of consolidation and the holding of annual meetings in rotation in all principal cities west of the Alleghenies was treated with derision and they were informed that if they saw fit they could join the St. Louis association but no union or any plan by which meetings would be held elsewhere than in St. Louis would be considered. The St. Louis meeting was also given up to but one idea, that of the national trail from Texas to Canada. There seemed to be no other object for the meeting. Also in this meeting Texas was given twenty-two votes. New Mexico twelve and only one to Wyoming, Nebraska and Dakota combined. The delegates from Wyoming association did not see fit to join the St. Louis association and went back to Chicago and joined the National Cattlegrowers' association of America, in which Wyoming is entitled to about forty votes. It was also reported that the commissoner of animal industry has been empowered by congress to expend his fund of $100,000 at his own discretion. This can now be used toward buying infected animals and thus stop almost any disease in its infancy. On the subject of transportation it was reported that both the Union and Northern Pacific had made reductions of five per cent., thus effecting a saving of about six dollars a car or a total of $72,000 on cattle shipped by members of the association. In regard to mavericks it was found that $26,000 had been derived from their sale. In every case but one, good prices had been paid. In the matter of inspectors, it was estimated that over a million cattle have been looked after by them since April, 1884. 2,779 strays were picked up at the different shipping points making a total saving to the association of $108,000. Many disturbances and in fact the possibility of many members resigning and forming new associations were finally settled harmoniously. All the old officers were elected for the ensuing year, the member of the executive committee for Dakota being Dorr Clark, of the E 6 and V V V outfits.
articles.summary: Report of the Wyoming Stock-growers' Association meeting at Cheyenne: Texas fever, quarantine, national association split, freight reductions, and Dorr Clark named Dakota's executive committee member.

articles.text: With those elected at the last meeting the Wyoming association has 461 members. The Montana association is close on her heels and will catch up inside of two year.
articles.summary: Wyoming association membership reaches 461.

articles.text: The committee appointed by the Wyoming association to look up the bull question were unanimously in favor of taking up and feeding them from December to July. In one case this action increased the calf crop to 85 per cent. and the beeves when sold averaged fifty pounds heavier than others.
articles.summary: Wyoming committee favors taking up and feeding bulls in winter.

articles.text: In the year 1884 Chicago received 1,817,697 cattle; 801,630 sheep; 5,351,967 hogs and 18,602 horses. In nineteen years she has received 103,333,532 head of live stock, valued at $2,074,127,503. The report of the Chamber of commerce reports that the fresh beef trade is steadily increasing, owing to the improved methods and facilities for carrying on the work. Owing to the foot-and-mouth disease scare last May the market was for a time very suggish but picked up later on and 1,118,154 cattle were killed for the dressed meat, canning and packing trade.
articles.summary: Chicago livestock receipts for 1884.

articles.text: In the report of Dr. Hopkins veterinarian of the Wyoming association, a cause of the death of states bulls and cattle was brought out that has escaped the notice of our cowmen. It was supposed that states cattle die in larger numbers than others because the cold was more intense and the feed of a different kind. It appears that they do not die as much from this reason, however, as from the fact that these changes bring diseases, common to all pilgrims on the range. The fact has now been established beyond all doubt that bulls and especially pilgrims, cannot run with the herd the whole year without serious loss. They must be taken up and fed. If they are not, disease in some shape and death are sure to attack them. In view of this fact, we prophesy that the time is close at hand when the cowmen will see it is to their interest to not only take up their bulls for seven or eight months in the year, but also to feed them well and give them some kind of a shelter besides a wire fence.
articles.summary: Packard urges cowmen to take up, feed and shelter bulls, citing Dr. Hopkins' report.

articles.text: The question of leasing public lands is getting to be one of great importance in Indian territory and one that we think should be decided in favor of leasing. At first sight it would seem that this would be entirely for the benefit of large capitalists and would creat a virtual monopoly in the leased districts. There are two sides to the question, however and the other side is that the lands in question are generally desert or virtually so on account of the lack of water. No one is going to put improvements on public lands when they are liable at any time to be driven off and the only way to make this land productive is to lease it for a term of years with the privilege of buying at the end of the lease. Plenty of water will then be obtained in wells and what are now deserts will become as good grazing land as any. Again the inevitable tendency of the cow business is toward monopoly. By the leasing of lands many smaller outfits will be given a good show, where now they will soon be crowded to the wall. For these and many other reasons the Cow Boy is in favor of leasing any and all public lands that can by any construction, come under the Desert land act.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy comes out in favor of leasing public grazing lands.

articles.text: In all cattle papers the question of hornless cattle is being discussed. Numbers and testimony are immensely in their favor and the question has now narrowed down to the point as to whether it is better or not to dehorn cattle. The evidence is strongly in favor of this, but in reference to range cattle we are still in the dark as to whether it would pay. There is scarcely any doubt, however, that it would pay in the case of calves. As to naturally hornless or polled cattle, it is past dispute that they make by far the best beef-producing and range cattle. Almost without exception Aberdeen-Angus took the first prize in the block contest in all fat stock shows, the most noticable victories of this year being the national contest at Smithfield, England and the international contest at New Orleans. Among the polls, however, there is quite a rivalry as to which is the better for the range, Galloways or Aberdeen-Angus. The Galloways have longer hair and may be able to stand greater cold, but the Aberdeen-Angus have repeatedly shown their ability to stand any kind of weather with perfect ease, so that on account of the superior record of the Angus for beef-producing qualities, we still hold them as the coming prime favorites for the range. They have been a long time gaining their present popularity but are certain of its being increased. A strong point in their favor is that any one who handles them is immediately an uncompromising partisan in their favor. In some late cattle sales we notice that T. C. Powers, of Ft. Benton, a pioneer in Angus cattle for the range, recently bought a number in Chicago and J. J. Hill, of St. Paul bought a small herd in Scotland. We are glad also to see that our stockmen are realizing the value of Aberdeen-Angus bulls. There are several now on the river and the LeMoyne cattle Co. will put in either Angus or Galloway bulls this season. Clemmer & Dell, of Cave Hills, have a number, their best bull costing $600. The name of their company is the Aberdeen-Angus cattle Co. Sam Wallace, formerly of Glendive is puting in cattle below Howard Eaton's ranch and the Co. will be called the Angus cattle Co.
articles.summary: On hornless and polled cattle; favors Aberdeen-Angus, noting local herds of Angus bulls (LeMoyne Co., Clemmer & Dell, Sam Wallace).

Ready-print page: a column headed "The Bad Lands Cow Boy, A. T. Packard, Publisher" carrying syndicated editorials (cholera, mercantile failures, Bazaine, Henry Ward Beecher), Summary of News of the Week, a biographical sketch of General U. S. Grant, foreign news, Dakota Territorial Notes, and serial fiction "The Ring and the Mirror."

Ready-print page: fiction and poetry, miscellany (longevity of men and women, stage peculiarities), and patent-medicine and mail-order advertisements (Cuticura, Tutt's Pills, Hostetter's Bitters, St. Jacobs Oil, Kidney-Wort, etc.).

articles.summary: Stage line and Northern Pacific time tables at Medora; page masthead dated Thursday, April 16, 1885.

articles.text: No. 2 was about eleven hours late yesterday.
articles.summary: The eastbound Atlantic Express was eleven hours late.

articles.text: Just stop a minute and listen to the hammers.
articles.summary: Building activity in Medora.

articles.text: Bob Roberts is on his way home, being now in New York.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts in New York on his way home.

articles.text: John Warn expects to return from Bozeman in about ten days.
articles.summary: John Warn expected back from Bozeman.

articles.text: B. F. Lamb has decided that his new brand shall be BL connected.
articles.summary: B. F. Lamb adopts a connected BL brand.

articles.text: A new barn for the accommodation of stage and other stock is nearly completed.
articles.summary: New stage barn nearly done.

articles.text: Nothing has been heard from J. D. Garver, since he went to Bismarck to see his wife and it is feared she may be seriously ill.
articles.summary: J. D. Garver went to Bismarck to see his wife, feared seriously ill.

articles.text: Sam. Whitney has decided to make Medora his home and has gone to housekeeping in Bob Roberts building. His eldest daughter arrived last evening.
articles.summary: Sam Whitney settles in Medora; his eldest daughter arrived.

articles.text: It is perfectly wonderful, the change that even the little rain of last night effected. Everywhere now can be seen the tinge of the rapidly growing grass.
articles.summary: A little rain fell last night and the grass is greening.

articles.text: The LeMoyne cattle Co. will soon ship in one or two car loads of bulls. From letters of Mr. LeMoyne, we judge that they will be grade Galloways or Aberdeen-Angus.
articles.summary: LeMoyne Cattle Co. to ship in carloads of Galloway or Angus bulls.

articles.text: E. G. Paddock's livery stable is completed and, as predicted, is by no means a detriment to the looks of the town. He has already opened up and in a few days will be able to meet nearly any demand made on him.
articles.summary: E. G. Paddock's livery stable completed and open.

articles.text: The whole of the plateau east of town burned over Monday evening, the fire spreading in all directions. We wish to remark that the reward of $250 for the arrest and conviction of anyone setting the grass on fire still holds good.
articles.summary: Prairie fire burned the plateau east of Medora Monday evening.

articles.text: Several times we have heard the question asked as to whether the stage line would get a mail contract. Bids were advertised for last February and the first day of July will surely see a mail go out of Medora for the Hills.
articles.summary: Mail service by stage to the Black Hills expected July 1.

articles.text: None of the contestants have shot off their back scores in the shooting match. Two members of the executive committee are to make up back scores and as the president was out of town it had to be postponed last Saturday. Weather permitting, the scores will be shot next Saturday.
articles.summary: Shooting-match back scores postponed to next Saturday.

articles.text: Much improvement work is being done at the coal mine. An air shaft is being tunnelled, a new chute built, tracks and coal buggy added and many more improvements. The expenses have already gone beyond the receipts, but it is hoped that a contract made for all the coal the Co. uses and next winter's trade will straighten matters.
articles.summary: Improvements at the Medora coal mine.

articles.text: G. G. Cooper, formerly day operator here, went to Billings Monday night to accept a corresponding position there. We are pleased at his promotion but sorry to lose him as he made many friends here, not particularly on account of his good looks, but more by reason of his "winning ways." W. H. Fortier, of Gladstone, relieves him here.
articles.summary: Telegraph operator G. G. Cooper transferred to Billings; W. H. Fortier replaces him.

articles.text: Tom Jones passed through Medora last night on his way to Tacoma. He will return as soon as possible. His trip probably has some connection with work on the extensions of the N. P. He reports that capitalists are become interested and mean business in reference to the Hay creek coal road. Joe Pennell is in charge of the aqueduct work in New York.
articles.summary: Tom Jones passed through en route to Tacoma; reports interest in the Hay Creek coal road.

articles.text: James W. Allen arrived from Deadwood yesterday morning and immediately entered upon the duties of superintendent to which office he was appointed by John A. Gaston, who is now General manager. This looks more like business than any move that has been made for some time. The way to secure patronage is to place authority in the hands of men who are well-known in the Hills and who know how to rustle. These requisites are both filled by Messrs. Gaston and Allen. We learn also, that in all minor affairs, full power is put in the hands of the manager and superintendent the only way in which the line can be run satisfactorily. We now will prophesy that our line will do a much better business than formerly
articles.summary: James W. Allen takes over as superintendent of the Medora–Black Hills stage line under general manager John A. Gaston.

articles.text: In spite of the rain the masquerade last night was a complete success. Nearly thirty were masked, some of them being strikingly original. That of Mrs. Elmer was perhaps the best, but as she did not skate, she was out of the contest. The first prize was won by Miss Maggie Guardient and second by Polly Fitzgerald. The first prize among the gentlemen was won by Martin Timlin. First prizes are three-week's skating tickets, second, a week's ticket. The calling and playing of F. Bernan were very satisfactory, he introducing several new and pleasing movements in the dancing, which began at ten o'clock, the maskers having about exhausted themselves on skates, trying to disguise their movements. The masquerade will be repeated shortly.
articles.summary: Masquerade skating party at the rink a success; prizes to Maggie Guardient, Polly Fitzgerald and Martin Timlin.

articles.text: Arbor day has been postponed to April 25th by order of governor Pierce.
articles.summary: Arbor Day postponed to April 25 by Gov. Pierce.

articles.text: B. F. Lamb is making many improvements on his ranch and will soon be in shape to receive cattle.
articles.summary: B. F. Lamb improving his ranch.

articles.text: W. B. Pryor's boot and shoe business has opened up in good shape and he is now on the lookout for a shoemaker.
articles.summary: W. B. Pryor's boot and shoe shop opened.

articles.text: Two wagon loads of leather goods for the Glendive branch of J. S. Collins' Cheyenne house, passed through Medora last Saturday.
articles.summary: Leather goods for J. S. Collins' Glendive branch freighted through Medora.

articles.text: Postmaster Gallup, of Cave Hills, came up last week on business. He reports the loss of cattle in Cave Hills at a little more than average, the Hash-Knife outfit being the heaviest losers.
articles.summary: Cave Hills cattle losses a little above average; Hash-Knife hardest hit.

articles.text: A number of subscribers will miss the Cow Boy owing to our motto: "Cash or no Cow Boy." There are still a few delinquent local subscribers who are requested to call at their earliest convenience.
articles.summary: Cow Boy cuts off non-paying subscribers.

articles.text: C. S. Grindall went east Sunday morning accompanied by his family. He intends buying between five hundred and a thousand States cattle for his Beaver creek ranch. He reported that there was an enjoyable dance at Mingusville Friday night.
articles.summary: C. S. Grindall went east to buy States cattle; reports a dance at Mingusville.

articles.text: If present indications hold out, Medora will soon have a gold mine craze. Messrs. Martin and Keeler recently panned out about twenty cents in one pan of dirt up the river. This is excellent pay and if it holds out will make first class diggings.
articles.summary: Martin and Keeler pan gold up the Little Missouri.

articles.text: There is a good deal of uncertainty in reference to the stockyards to be built here. They were at first laid out on a liberal plan and afterwards the corrall was contracted to 50x50 feet. This was again changed to a hundred feet square and now again the dimensions are uncertain.
articles.summary: Uncertainty over the dimensions of the Medora stockyards.

articles.text: Rev. J. B. Schaffner preached again last Sunday night at the rink. His sermon was an eloquent one and well deserving of a larger audience. Probably the reason that so few attended was that it was doubtful if Mr. Schaffner would arrive. Hereafter there will be no doubt as he has made arrangements to come every Sunday evening. Hereafter also there will be better music as his organ will be in the rink. Let every one turn out Sunday evening.
articles.summary: Rev. J. B. Schaffner preached at the rink and will hold services every Sunday evening.

articles.text: One of the worst wrecks for a small one that it has ever been our lot to see, occurred Saturday afternoon, four-and-a-half miles west of here. A steer thought he was "as big a man as the engine" and came nearly proving it, the effect being disastrous on both sides. The engine and tender were completely disabled and ditched, four empty freight cars were badly demoralized and two more ran off the track. C. S. Grindall, of the E S G Beaver creek ranch, engineer White and the fireman were in the cab and all escaped unharmed, though how they did it after seeing the wreck, is a mystery. The loss will be about $4,000.
articles.summary: A steer derailed a Northern Pacific train 4½ miles west of Medora; about $4,000 loss, no injuries.

articles.text: Levi Deffebach came in Monday from the bull round-up north of the track. The bulls were in splendid condition as were all the cattle. There will be a large calf crop, which may reach 75 per cent. The most encouraging thing about the round-up was the few dead cattle found. Only eight were found on ranges over which about 8,000 cattle graze. This again puts us all at sea in reference to loss but it makes us all the more certain that it will fall far below three per cent. There isn't another range in the United States that shows up like the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Levi Deffebach reports the bull round-up north of the track found cattle in splendid condition and only eight dead.

articles.summary: Directory of display and cattle-brand advertisements on page 4, including Theodore Roosevelt's Chimney Butte (Maltese Cross) Ranch brand.

events.date_basis: Brand ad in Thu 16 Apr 1885 issue
events.title: Chimney Butte Ranch brand advertised: Theodore Roosevelt, proprietor
events.summary: The Cow Boy carried the brand notice of the Chimney Butte Ranch, Theodore Roosevelt proprietor, with Ferris & Merrifield as managers, ranging six miles south of the railroad on the Little Missouri.
events.excerpt: Chimney Butte Ranch. Theodore Roosevelt, Proprietor. Ferris & Merrifield, Managers.

events.title: Steer wrecks a train four and a half miles west of Medora
events.summary: A steer struck a train west of Medora, ditching the engine and tender and derailing freight cars; C. S. Grindall, engineer White and the fireman escaped unharmed. Loss about $4,000.
events.excerpt: A steer thought he was "as big a man as the engine" and came nearly proving it

events.title: Prairie fire burns plateau east of Medora
events.summary: The whole plateau east of town burned over, the fire spreading in all directions; the $250 reward for anyone setting grass fires still stands.
events.excerpt: The whole of the plateau east of town burned over Monday evening

events.title: Masquerade skating party at the rink
events.summary: Nearly thirty maskers attended a masquerade at the rink; prizes went to Maggie Guardient, Polly Fitzgerald and Martin Timlin, with dancing called by F. Bernan.
events.excerpt: In spite of the rain the masquerade last night was a complete success.

events.title: Rain greens the grass around Medora
events.summary: A little rain fell and the grass began greening rapidly.
events.excerpt: the change that even the little rain of last night effected

events.title: James W. Allen becomes stage line superintendent
events.summary: James W. Allen arrived from Deadwood to take up the superintendency of the Medora–Black Hills stage line, appointed by general manager John A. Gaston.
events.excerpt: James W. Allen arrived from Deadwood yesterday morning and immediately entered upon the duties of superintendent

events.title: Levi Deffebach reports on bull round-up north of the track
events.summary: Deffebach came in from the bull round-up north of the railroad; cattle were in splendid condition and only eight dead were found on ranges grazing about 8,000 head.
events.excerpt: There isn't another range in the United States that shows up like the Bad Lands.

events.title: Bull round-up south of the track begins
events.summary: The bull round-up south of the railroad began, working Davis, Sully, Andrews and Garner creeks; few dead animals found.
events.excerpt: The bull round-up south of the track began Tuesday.

events.title: Little Missouri round-up set for May 25
events.summary: The Little Missouri round-up was announced to begin May 25.
events.excerpt: The Little Missouri round-up begins May 25.

events.title: Telegraph operator G. G. Cooper leaves for Billings
events.summary: Day operator G. G. Cooper went to Billings for a corresponding position; W. H. Fortier of Gladstone replaced him at Medora.
events.excerpt: W. H. Fortier, of Gladstone, relieves him here.

events.title: Tom Jones passes through Medora en route to Tacoma
events.summary: Tom Jones passed through on his way to Tacoma and reported capitalists interested in the Hay Creek coal road.
events.excerpt: capitalists are become interested and mean business in reference to the Hay creek coal road

events.title: C. S. Grindall goes east to buy States cattle
events.summary: Grindall left with his family to buy 500 to 1,000 States cattle for his Beaver Creek ranch.
events.excerpt: He intends buying between five hundred and a thousand States cattle for his Beaver creek ranch.

events.title: Dance at Mingusville
events.summary: C. S. Grindall reported an enjoyable dance at Mingusville.
events.excerpt: there was an enjoyable dance at Mingusville Friday night

events.title: Rev. J. B. Schaffner preaches at the rink
events.summary: Rev. Schaffner preached at the rink to a small audience and arranged to come every Sunday evening, bringing his organ.
events.excerpt: he has made arrangements to come every Sunday evening

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 16 Apr 1885 issue
events.title: Gold panned up the Little Missouri
events.summary: Messrs. Martin and Keeler panned about twenty cents in one pan of dirt up the river, raising talk of a gold craze.
events.excerpt: Medora will soon have a gold mine craze.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 16 Apr 1885 issue
events.title: E. G. Paddock's livery stable opens
events.summary: Paddock's livery stable was completed and opened.
events.excerpt: E. G. Paddock's livery stable is completed

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 16 Apr 1885 issue
events.title: W. B. Pryor opens boot and shoe business
events.summary: Pryor's boot and shoe business opened and he sought a shoemaker.
events.excerpt: W. B. Pryor's boot and shoe business has opened up in good shape

events.title: Leather goods for J. S. Collins' Glendive branch pass through Medora
events.summary: Two wagon loads of leather goods for the Glendive branch of J. S. Collins' Cheyenne house passed through.
events.excerpt: Two wagon loads of leather goods for the Glendive branch

events.title: Postmaster Gallup of Cave Hills reports cattle losses
events.summary: Gallup came up on business and reported Cave Hills cattle losses a little above average, the Hash-Knife outfit losing most.
events.excerpt: the Hash-Knife outfit being the heaviest losers

events.title: Arbor Day postponed to April 25 by Governor Pierce
events.summary: Arbor Day was postponed to April 25 by order of the territorial governor.
events.excerpt: Arbor day has been postponed to April 25th by order of governor Pierce.

events.title: Doc. Pennell leaves for the Black Hills with tree sprouts
events.summary: Doc. Pennell loaded up and left for the Hills with tree sprouts and shrubs.
events.excerpt: Doc. Pennell loaded and pulled for the Hills last Saturday

events.title: Wm. VanDriesche returns
events.summary: Wm. VanDriesche returned Monday evening.
events.excerpt: Wm. VanDriesche returned Monday evening.

events.title: Willard Bros. expected with eighty cow-horses
events.summary: The Willard Bros. were expected with eighty head of cow-horses to sell on the river.
events.excerpt: eighty head of cow-horses, which they hope to sell on the river

events.date_basis: "the first of next week" after Thu 16 Apr 1885
events.title: Dr. Jorgens to move into new drug store building
events.summary: Dr. Jorgens planned to move into his new 24x32 building with a full glass front and add crockery.
events.excerpt: The building is 24x32 and is to have a full glass front.

events.title: Sam Whitney settles in Medora
events.summary: Sam Whitney made Medora his home, keeping house in the Bob Roberts building; his eldest daughter arrived.
events.excerpt: Sam. Whitney has decided to make Medora his home

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 16 Apr 1885 issue
events.title: Improvements at the Medora coal mine
events.summary: An air shaft, new chute, tracks and coal buggy were being added at the coal mine.
events.excerpt: An air shaft is being tunnelled, a new chute built

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 16 Apr 1885 issue
events.title: Uncertainty over Medora stockyards
events.summary: The planned stockyards' dimensions had changed several times and remained uncertain.
events.excerpt: now again the dimensions are uncertain

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 16 Apr 1885 issue
events.title: Medora slaughter house nearly ready
events.summary: The slaughter house was nearly ready, hoping to start by May 1.
events.excerpt: The slaughter house is nearly ready for business

events.date_basis: "the first day of July" stated in text
events.title: Stage mail to the Black Hills expected July 1
events.summary: The paper expected a mail contract to send mail out of Medora for the Hills by July 1.
events.excerpt: the first day of July will surely see a mail go out of Medora for the Hills

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 16 Apr 1885 issue
events.title: LeMoyne Cattle Co. to import Galloway or Angus bulls
events.summary: LeMoyne Cattle Co. planned to ship in one or two carloads of bulls.
events.excerpt: they will be grade Galloways or Aberdeen-Angus

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 16 Apr 1885 issue
events.title: Nothing heard from J. D. Garver
events.summary: J. D. Garver had gone to Bismarck to see his wife, who was feared seriously ill.
events.excerpt: it is feared she may be seriously ill

events.title: Atlantic Express No. 2 eleven hours late
events.summary: No. 2 was about eleven hours late.
events.excerpt: No. 2 was about eleven hours late yesterday.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 16 Apr 1885 issue
events.title: Dorr Clark named Dakota member of Wyoming association executive committee
events.summary: At the Wyoming Stock-growers' meeting at Cheyenne, Dorr Clark of the E6 and VVV outfits was named Dakota's executive committee member.
events.excerpt: the member of the executive committee for Dakota being Dorr Clark

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 16 Apr 1885 issue
events.title: Bismarck city election goes Democratic
events.summary: John A. Carland was elected mayor of Bismarck.
events.excerpt: John A. Carland was elected mayor

events.title: Shooting match back scores postponed
events.summary: Back scores in the shooting match were postponed because the president was out of town; to be shot next Saturday.
events.excerpt: the scores will be shot next Saturday
